messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 25
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Journalist
  trauma_type: Police
  pcl5: 76

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Trauma-Related Events: Trauma-related events, Auditory (Footsteps): Footsteps behind or nearby, Certain Songs: Certain songs
  Maladaptive Strategies: Concealing Clothing: wear concealing clothing to avoid being noticed, Avoid Grief Reminders: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost, Avoid All Feelings: avoid anything that could cause negative or positive feelings
  Threat: Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
  Memory: More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things, Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma, No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kofi was twenty-three years old and working as a freelance journalist in a mid-sized American city when he was pulled over during a routine traffic stop that became anything but routine. He had been driving home late from covering a city council meeting, his laptop bag on the passenger seat, a half-finished article about housing policy still open on his phone. The officer approached his window and asked for his license and registration. Kofi reached for the glove compartment, and in that moment—he still could not fully explain why—the officer drew his weapon and ordered him out of the car at gunpoint. Kofi was forced to the ground, his hands cuffed behind his back, his face pressed into the cold asphalt while the officer shouted questions he could not answer coherently. The whole incident lasted perhaps twelve minutes. He was released with a warning. But those twelve minutes had rewritten everything.

What stayed with Kofi most vividly was not the visual image of the gun, though that was burned into his mind. It was the sound. The officer’s boots on the pavement as he approached. The sharp metallic click of the handcuffs. And later, when he tried to describe it to his girlfriend, he found he could not get the words out. He would start the story, reach the part where the officer’s voice changed, and then the thread would vanish. His mouth would go dry. He would lose the sentence entirely and have to stop. The memory itself, however, never lost its vividness. It felt more real than anything that had happened since. Sometimes, without warning, he would be standing at the kitchen counter making coffee and he would hear the officer’s footsteps again, clear as day, coming up behind him from the hallway. He would spin around, heart hammering, only to find an empty corridor.

In the months that followed, Kofi’s life contracted. He had always been someone who moved through the world with ease—a journalist who loved the unpredictability of the streets, the hum of a new neighborhood, the challenge of finding a story in an unfamiliar place. Now, he found himself avoiding unfamiliar neighborhoods entirely. He could not assess the danger in a place he did not already know, and that uncertainty felt intolerable. He began checking behind him constantly, especially when walking to his car or waiting for the subway. He started wearing hooded sweatshirts and dark, shapeless coats—clothing that let him blend in, that made him harder to notice. He told himself it was practical. But he knew, deep down, that he was trying to become invisible.

His work suffered. He stopped taking assignments that required him to go to parts of the city he had not scouted in advance. He turned down a story about police accountability—the irony was not lost on him—because the thought of sitting in a precinct and interviewing officers made his chest tighten until he could barely breathe. He had difficulty concentrating during interviews now; his mind would drift to the sound of footsteps in the hallway outside the room, and he would miss what the source was saying. His editor noticed. His girlfriend noticed. He noticed most of all.

He had come to believe, quietly and without ever saying it aloud, that his life had been destroyed by those twelve minutes. He used to be a happy person. He remembered that version of himself the way you remember a photograph of someone you used to know. That person was gone. He was no longer capable of doing the things that had defined him—the curiosity, the courage, the willingness to go anywhere for a story. He avoided anything that might make him feel, whether positive or negative, because feelings felt dangerous now. He even avoided songs that reminded him of a friend he had lost years ago, not because the grief was fresh, but because any emotional intensity felt like a door he did not want to open.

What finally brought Kofi to seek help was a moment that frightened him more than the traffic stop itself. He was at a stoplight, his girlfriend in the passenger seat, when a police cruiser pulled up alongside them. The officer glanced over. Kofi’s hands went numb on the wheel. He heard boots on pavement, a voice shouting, the click of metal. He pulled over and began to cry, and he could not explain to his girlfriend why. He could not explain to himself. He came to therapy because he was afraid of what he might do next time—not to someone else, but to himself, to the life he was still trying to hold together. He wanted to know if the person he used to be was still in there somewhere, or if that person had been erased for good.
